n: The famine reached Canaan. Jacob hears there is grain in Egypt and scolds his sons for standing around staring at one another instead of acting.
Jacob sends his sons to Egypt to buy grain so the family can survive. Without knowing it, he is sending them to Joseph.

f.w: that we may live, and not die

n: Ten brothers go down—the same ten who sold Joseph into Egypt years before.
Jacob kept Benjamin home. Benjamin was Rachel’s other son, and Jacob now protected him the way he once favored Joseph.
Jacob’s sons joined the crowds of foreigners traveling to Egypt for food.
As governor, Joseph personally oversaw grain sales. His brothers bowed with faces to the ground—literally fulfilling Joseph’s dream of the sheaves.
Joseph recognized them immediately but disguised himself and spoke harshly. He needed to learn whether they had changed.

f.g: acted like a stranger, disguised himself

n: About twenty years had passed; Joseph now looked, dressed, and spoke like an Egyptian official, so they did not recognize him.
Remembering his dreams, Joseph accused them of spying—searching out Egypt’s weak points. The test had begun.
The brothers protest: they came only to buy food.
They insist they are honest men, all sons of one father. The irony is sharp—these “honest men” had deceived their father for years.
Joseph repeats the accusation to press them further.
Under pressure they reveal family details: twelve brothers, the youngest at home, and “one is not.” Joseph hears how they speak of him.
Joseph holds to his charge, keeping them off balance.
Joseph sets the test: they must bring the youngest brother. He swears “by the life of Pharaoh,” speaking as an Egyptian would.

f.g: This is how you will be tested

n: At first Joseph proposes keeping nine in prison and sending one home for Benjamin.
Joseph puts all ten in custody for three days—a small taste of what he had endured.
On the third day Joseph softens the plan and assures them he fears God—a hint they might have caught, had they been listening.

f.g: I revere God and act with integrity

n: Now only one brother would stay behind while the rest carried food to their hungry families.
They must return with Benjamin to prove their story. They agreed.
Their guilt rose to the surface. They remembered Joseph’s anguish and pleading from the pit and concluded they were reaping what they had sown. Their consciences were awakening.
Reuben reminds them he had warned them not to harm the boy. Now, he says, they must answer for his blood.

f.g: we are being held accountable for his death

n: They spoke freely in Hebrew, not knowing Joseph understood every word, since he used an interpreter.
Joseph turned away and wept. Then he chose Simeon, the second oldest, and bound him in front of them. Some suggest Simeon was chosen because Reuben had tried to save Joseph.
Joseph secretly returned their payment in their sacks and gave them supplies for the journey—mercy hidden inside a test.
The brothers loaded their donkeys with grain and set out for home.
At a rest stop, one brother opened his sack to feed his donkey and found his money right at the top.

f.g: a camping place along the road, not a hotel

n: Their hearts sank. They feared they would be accused of theft, and they sensed God was dealing with them: “What is this that God hath done unto us?”
Back in Canaan they told Jacob everything that had happened.
They describe the stern lord of Egypt who accused them of spying.
They repeat their defense: they are honest men.
They explain they told him about their family, including the missing brother and the youngest at home.
They explain the condition: one brother had to stay behind as a pledge.
If they bring Benjamin, Simeon will be released and they may trade freely in Egypt.
As they emptied their sacks, every man found his money. Now even Jacob was afraid of what it meant.
Jacob bursts out in grief: Joseph is gone, Simeon is gone, and now they want Benjamin. “All these things are against me”—though, in truth, all things were working for him.

f.w: all these things are against me

n: Reuben makes a rash offer: kill my two sons if I fail to bring Benjamin back. It shows sincerity but not wisdom.
Jacob refuses. Benjamin is the only son left of Rachel; losing him would send Jacob to the grave in sorrow. Judah will offer a wiser pledge in the next chapter.

f.w: bring down my gray hairs with sorrow to the grave
f.g: cause my death in grief as an old man
Hebrew Sheol, the world of the dead
